name: Treaty with the Oneida, 1838
aka: Treaty with the First Christian and Orchard parties of the Oneida
nations: Oneida Nation (Wisconsin), the First Christian and Orchard parties at Green Bay
promises: Article 2: from the land ceded, a reservation of 100 acres for each individual, held as other Indian lands are held, drawn to include all Oneida settlements and improvements near Green Bay (surveyed at about 65,000 acres).
Article 3: $3,000 to the Orchard party and $30,500 to the First Christian party, of which $3,000 could go to a church and parsonage.
Article 5: the United States would pay the expenses of the treaty and of the delegation.
compensation: No Indian Claims Commission award was found for this treaty. In Docket 159 the Commission dismissed the Oneida Tribe of Wisconsin's claim that the United States failed to protect reservation timber (12 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, December 6, 1962).
today: On July 30, 2020 the Seventh Circuit held that Congress never diminished or disestablished the reservation created by this treaty, so the entire 1838 reservation remains Indian country, even though allotment beginning under the Dawes Act let much of the land pass out of Indian hands (Oneida Nation v. Village of Hobart, No. 19-1981).

sources.title: Oneida Tribe of Indians of Wisconsin v. United States, Docket 159, Opinion of the Commission, December 6, 1962
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

sources.title: Oneida Nation v. Village of Hobart, No. 19-1981 (7th Cir. July 30, 2020)
sources.publisher: Turtle Talk (Michigan State University College of Law), copy of the slip opinion

openQuestions: Loss of most of the reservation through allotment and fee patents (the General Allotment Act and the 1906 act that allowed fee patents on Oneida allotments) is the main lead. The 2020 ruling held those acts did not shrink the reservation, but whether any finding treats the land loss as a breach of Article 2 was not found.
The Seventh Circuit noted expert reports by Frederick Hoxie and R. David Edmunds on the reservation's history (ECF 92-2 and 92-5); they were not opened.
The Oneida Nation's own account of the 1838 treaty (oneida-nsn.gov) was not found in this pass.
Royce's states field for this queue entry (WI) is right, but treaties.json lists New York nations as present-day tribes for it; only the Oneida Nation of Wisconsin was party.
